title: Restart the web application
content:
Use Nexus Control, never a shell, for routine restarts.

  1. Sign in as an Operator and open Nexus Control.
  2. Choose nexus-web and confirm the restart.
  3. Wait one minute and check Nexus Status.

If the status stays red, roll back with the steps in the rollback runbook.

title: Roll back a release
content:
A rollback swaps the current and previous release folders and restarts the web application.

  1. Ask an Administrator to run the rollback script on the server.
  2. Check /api/health/ready returns ready.
  3. Write down why you rolled back.

title: The Starting Point
content:
The project began with an existing Rocky Linux host (Nexus Core 01) containing various disconnected, buggy prototype drafts and legacy test scripts left over from earlier explorations. These older prototypes suffered from critical security and reliability flaws: hardcoded passwords, plaintext credential files, exposed unauthenticated web interfaces, and fragile monolithic scripts.

Rather than patching broken legacy code, the project owner decided on a clean-slate greenfield approach: inspect the older drafts solely to understand business requirements, safely archive the old environment after an exhaustive verified backup, and engineer a brand-new, enterprise-grade unified platform from first principles.

title: Architecture Decisions: The Cohesive Single Host
content:
YTL Nexus is architected as a single Next.js 16.3.5 web application paired with carefully selected, battle-tested system daemons running on one Rocky Linux server. Key architectural choices include:

  • Next.js App Router: Server Components by default, strict role-based access control with server-side guards, and atomic client transitions.
  • Dual-Mode Adapters: Every underlying service adapter (database, auth, mail, SFTPGo, Prometheus, Ollama, operations agent) implements both a live and a deterministic demo mode selectable via NEXUS_MODE.
  • Zero-Bypass Reverse Proxy: Apache acts as the hardened TLS termination gateway, delegating API and page traffic to Next.js while protecting loopback-only service sockets.
  • Append-Only Audit Logging: Every authenticated and state-modifying action is permanently recorded in a dedicated audit log table.

title: Challenges Overcome
content:
Unifying seven distinct infrastructure subsystems onto a single production host presented significant real-world engineering hurdles:

  • Hardened Local IPC: Connecting Next.js securely to local host daemons without granting unconstrained root privileges required building a scoped UNIX domain socket agent (nexus-ops) authenticated with HMAC request signatures and timestamp validation.
  • Headless Content Pipeline: Bridging WordPress headless REST endpoints with Next.js static and dynamic caching using cryptographically signed revalidation webhooks.
  • Hardware Resource Constraints: Tuning the local Gemma 3 Ollama model and node_exporter metrics polling so that background tasks and indexing do not degrade real-time web responsiveness on constrained virtual CPUs.
  • Automated Continuity Verification: Constructing self-verifying backup scripts with automated restore drills testing checksums and table counts against scratch databases.

title: Security Lessons Learned
content:
Security was not retrofitted at the end—it was enforced from Task 1 onwards:

  • Never Trust the Client: Hidden URLs and client-side UI toggles are never security controls. Every layout, route handler, and server function validates user role authorization via requireRole() on the server.
  • Defense in Depth: Database accounts are segregated with least privilege (e.g. nexus_ingest can only insert into backup and audit tables, with zero SELECT or DELETE capabilities).
  • Deterministic Posture Auditing: Nexus Shield continuously validates 11 host security benchmarks (including TLS expiry, open ports, SSH root-login flags, and backup freshness), converting raw systemd telemetry into prioritized remediation advice.

title: Skills & Technical Growth
content:
Throughout this internship, the project demanded rigorous full-stack systems engineering rather than isolated frontend coding. Core competencies developed include:

  • Advanced Linux systems administration (systemd service units, timers, polkit policies, journalctl parsing, and PAM/SELinux security postures).
  • Modern Next.js 16 App Router architecture, TypeScript strict type safety, and Test-Driven Development (TDD) using Vitest and Playwright.
  • Database schema design, zero-downtime migration scripts, and transactional integrity with Kysely and MariaDB.
  • Automated infrastructure testing, cryptographic credential management, and WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility compliance.

content:
Use the Open Roundcube Webmail button on this page or go directly to /webmail/. Sign in with your full mailbox address (e.g. username@ytl-nexus.internal) and your mailbox password.

Webmail credentials are separate from your Nexus platform password. If you forgot your mailbox password, an Administrator can reset it in Nexus Control.

title: Configuring your email client
content:
You can connect desktop and mobile mail clients (such as Thunderbird, Apple Mail or Outlook) using standard IMAP and SMTP submission.

  • Incoming (IMAP): port 993, SSL/TLS required.
  • Outgoing (SMTP): port 587, STARTTLS required.
  • Username: your full email address (username@ytl-nexus.internal).
  • Authentication: Normal password.

Nexus uses certificates from the YTL Nexus internal CA. Make sure the CA certificate is installed on your client device.
